anf_compare.notes: Translated from the PG 74 Greek; no published English version was used for wording.

bible_refs.note: ἀποθνήσκομεν ... τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, καθὰ γέγραπται refers back to ἀπεθάνομεν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ (Romans 6:2; compare 6:11).
Full quotation: τὰ μέλη τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, πορνείαν, ἀκαθαρσίαν, πάθος, ἐπιθυμίαν κακὴν, καὶ τὴν πλεονεξίαν.
ὃ γὰρ ἀπέθανε τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, ἀπέθανεν ἐφάπαξ (Cyril's word order).
σύμφυτοι γεγόναμεν τῷ ὁμοιώματι τοῦ θανάτου αὐτοῦ ... καὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως.
New lemma: Τοῦτο γινώσκοντες ὅτι ὁ παλαιὸς ἡμῶν ἄνθρωπος κ.τ.λ.; τὸ σῶμα τῆς ἁμαρτίας, καταργούμενον and συνεσταυρώθη are taken from the same verse.

choices.why: ὁ τῆς ἁμαρτίας νόμος ('the law of sin') is Pauline language (Romans 7:23, 8:2) used as a term, not a quotation; not cited inline.

Ἑλλήνων ... τὴν δόξαν: the view that souls sinned before bodies and were given flesh as punishment; Cyril calls it the opinion of 'the Greeks' (pagan philosophy) and does not name anyone. No name is added.
παλαιὸς ἄνθρωπος rendered 'old self' (modern standard for Romans 6:6); παλαιότης τῆς ἐν Ἀδάμ rendered 'the old condition in Adam'.

choices.english: the Word who carried out the dispensation
choices.why: τοῦ οἰκονομοῦντος Λόγου rendered 'the Word who carried out the dispensation', as in 'the dispensation in the flesh' in u02-rem-early.

pass_a_gloss: [he died] according to flesh (κατὰ σάρκα) Christ, that he might loose (λύσῃ) the sin of the world; we die not according to the flesh — whence? — but to sin, as it is written, that is, showing (ἀποφαίνοντες) sin idle (ἀεργῆ) and inactive (ἄπρακτον) in ourselves through putting to death (κατανεκροῦν) the members on earth: fornication (πορνεία), uncleanness (ἀκαθαρσία), passion (πάθος), evil desire (ἐπιθυμία κακή), and covetousness (πλεονεξία). so we have become grown-together (σύμφυτοι) not only to the death of Christ according to flesh but also to the likeness (ὁμοίωμα) of his death. this would be understood as dying for (ὑπέρ) sin, and not for his own — far from it (πολλοῦ γε καὶ δεῖ); for God is blameless (ἄμωμος) and furthest from being able to offend (πλημμελεῖν); but, as I said, for the sin of the world: for what he died to sin, he died once for all (ἐφάπαξ). so we have become grown-together in the likeness of his death; we shall surely be grown-together and same-formed (ταυτοειδεῖς) also of his resurrection (ἀνάστασις); for we shall live in Christ, and the flesh will live again (ἀναβιώσεται), and we shall live in another manner too, having dedicated (ἀναθέντες) to him our own soul, being re-elemented/transformed (μεταστοιχειούμενοι) toward sanctification (ἁγιασμός) and into a glorious way of life (εὐκλεᾶ πολιτείαν) in the Holy Spirit. [lemma] knowing this, that our old man (παλαιὸς ἄνθρωπος) etc. who is our old man, what is the body of sin (σῶμα τῆς ἁμαρτίας) being abolished (καταργούμενον), in what manner was it co-crucified (συνεσταυρώθη) with Christ, necessary to inquire (πολυπραγμονεῖν). perhaps some will think the flesh from earth is called body of sin, as given in the order of penalty (ἐν τάξει δίκης) to the soul of man, because of having sinned even before bodies (πρὸ σωμάτων); for so it seems good to some to think and say; but the opinion (δόξα) being of the Greeks (Ἑλλήνων), let us thrust it away (διωσώμεθα) as not true. body of sin and our old man he calls the body from earth, having as it were from the oldness (παλαιότης) in Adam the necessity of being corrupted (καταφθείρεσθαι); for we were condemned (καταδεδικάσμεθα) in him as first; and besides being sick (ἠῤῥωστηκός) also in pleasure-loving (φιλήδονον); for so the flesh is by nature from implanted motions (ἐμφύτων κινημάτων). how then co-crucified with Christ? the Only-begotten (Μονογενής) became man and put on (ἠμπέσχετο) the flesh from earth, sick, as I said, unto death from the oldness in Adam, and travailing (ὠδίνουσαν) as it were in itself also with being whetted (ἀκονᾶσθαι) toward sin from implanted motions. the law of sin is at rest (κατηρεμεῖ) in the holy and all-pure (πανάγνῳ) flesh of Christ; and we do not say the more out-of-place (ἐκτοπώτερα) of human passions (παθῶν) were moved in him, except those having blameless (ἀδιάβλητον) movement: hungering, thirsting, toiling (κοπιᾶν), and what the law of nature has kept outside blame (αἰτίας) even in us. yet even if the law of sin was not moved in Christ, on account of being put to sleep (κατηυνᾶσθαι) by the power and activity (ἐνέργεια) of the economizing (οἰκονομοῦντος) Word, still when the nature of the flesh itself by itself is examined (δοκιμάζεται), even if understood in Christ, we shall find it not other than ours. so we have been co-crucified with him, his flesh having been crucified and as it were having the whole nature (ὅλην τὴν φύσιν) in itself; just as [continues u03-rem-mid]
pass_b_english: …Christ [died] according to the flesh, so that he might undo the sin of the world. We, however, do not die according to the flesh—how could we?—but to sin, as it is written (Romans 6:2); that is, we render sin idle and ineffective in ourselves by putting to death “the members that are on the earth: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and greed” (Colossians 3:5). We have been united, then, not merely with Christ’s death according to the flesh, but with the likeness of his death. And this would be understood as dying for sin, and not for his own sin—far from it! For God is blameless and utterly far from being able to do wrong. Rather, as I said, it was for the sin of the world: “For the death he died to sin, he died once for all” (Romans 6:10). So we have been united with him in the likeness of his death (Romans 6:5). And we shall certainly be united with him and share the same form in his resurrection as well, for we shall live in Christ. The flesh will come back to life, and we shall also live in another way, having dedicated our own souls to him and being transformed toward holiness and into a glorious way of life in the Holy Spirit.

“Knowing this, that our old self…,” and so on (Romans 6:6). Who is our old self, what is the body of sin that is done away with, and in what way was it crucified with Christ? We must look into this closely. Some will perhaps suppose that the earthly flesh is called the body of sin because it was given to the human soul by way of punishment, since the soul had sinned even before there were bodies; for that is how some think and speak. But since this opinion belongs to the Greeks, let us thrust it away as untrue.

By “body of sin” and “our old self,” then, he means the earthly body, which, from the old condition in Adam, must waste away into corruption; for we were condemned in him, the first man. Besides this, it is also sick with the love of pleasure, for that is how the flesh is by nature, because of its inborn impulses. How, then, was it crucified with Christ? The Only-begotten became man and clothed himself with the earthly flesh, which, as I said, had fallen sick with death because of the old condition in Adam, and which carried within itself, as if in labour, the tendency to be sharpened toward sin by its inborn impulses.

Yet the law of sin lies still in the holy and all-pure flesh of Christ. We certainly do not say that the more unseemly of the human passions were stirred in him, except those whose movement is blameless—I mean hunger and thirst and weariness, and whatever else the law of nature has kept free of blame even in us. Still, even though the law of sin was not stirred in Christ, because it was lulled to sleep by the power and working of the Word who carried out the dispensation, yet when the nature of the flesh is examined by itself, even if it is considered as it is in Christ, we shall find that it is no different from ours. So we were crucified with him when his flesh was crucified, flesh that held, as it were, the whole nature within itself; just as…

reviewer: claude (Wave A review, clause by clause against the Greek)
review_notes: Staged row fixed in place in tr0.json. Every clause checked against frm_u03_rem_source.json. (1) τὸ καταργούμενον: 'brought to nothing' changed to 'done away with', so it matches κατήργηται in u03-rem-mid ('Do you see, then, how the body of sin has been done away with?'), which answers this question. (2) δοκεῖ γὰρ ὧδέ τισι καὶ φρονεῖν καὶ λέγειν: 'some are pleased to think' overstated δοκεῖ; now 'that is how some think and speak'. (3) καταῤῥωστοῦσαν … τὸν θάνατον: 'sick unto death' was an archaism (KJV 'unto') and a John 11:4 echo Cyril does not make; now 'had fallen sick with death because of the old condition in Adam'. All else faithful: negation (οὐ κατά γε τὴν σάρκα; οὐχ ὑπέρ τε τῆς ἰδίας), the Greek pre-existence view rejected, Christ's blameless passions, the law of sin lulled by the Word, Scripture refs Romans 6:2, Colossians 3:5, Romans 6:10, 6:5, 6:6 correct.
Opens mid-sentence: the verb ἀπέθανε stands at the end of u03-open. '[died]' is bracketed as carried over from there; the leading ellipsis marks the join.
Ends mid-sentence at καθάπερ; u03-rem-mid continues ἀμέλει καὶ ἐν Ἀδάμ. The closing ellipsis marks the break.

οὐχὶ δὴ μόνον τῷ κατὰ σάρκα θανάτῳ Χριστοῦ: rendered literally 'not merely with Christ's death according to the flesh'. Cyril has just said that we do not die according to the flesh; μόνον may be a slip in the printed text, but nothing is changed.
ἵνα λύσῃ τοῦ κόσμου τὴν ἁμαρτίαν: possible echo of John 1:29 (τὴν ἁμαρτίαν τοῦ κόσμου), but the verb differs; left uncited as uncertain.
ὁ τῆς ἁμαρτίας νόμος ('the law of sin') is Pauline language (Romans 7:23, 8:2) used as a term, not a quotation; not cited inline.

Ἑλλήνων ... τὴν δόξαν: the view that souls sinned before bodies and were given flesh as punishment; Cyril calls it the opinion of 'the Greeks' (pagan philosophy) and does not name anyone. No name is added.
παλαιὸς ἄνθρωπος rendered 'old self' (modern standard for Romans 6:6); παλαιότης τῆς ἐν Ἀδάμ rendered 'the old condition in Adam'.
τοῦ οἰκονομοῦντος Λόγου rendered 'the Word who carried out the dispensation', as in 'the dispensation in the flesh' in u02-rem-early.
PG column numbers 191 and 192 and the page number 7 in the copy-text are dropped from the reading text.
